items.author: Sahara Vacation Team
items.title: Erg Chigaga vs Erg Chebbi: Which Moroccan Sahara Dunes Should You Choose?
items.content: Erg Chebbi and Erg Chigaga are Morocco's two great Saharan dune fields. This guide compares distance, access, crowds, trekking and price so you can pick the right desert tour for your trip.

body.text: Most travelers planning a Morocco desert tour end up weighing the same two names: Erg Chebbi, the famous golden wall of sand behind Merzouga, and Erg Chigaga, the wild, much quieter dune field that waits almost an hour of off-road track past M'Hamid El Ghizlane. Both are true Sahara, both end with a night under an absurd number of stars, and both will ruin ordinary beaches for you. But they deliver completely different experiences.

The short answer: choose Erg Chebbi if it is your first Sahara trip, your time is short, or you want an easy-to-reach classic dune sunset with the widest choice of camps. Choose Erg Chigaga if you want real remoteness, long camel treks, and a dune field you may have to yourself. You truly cannot go wrong — but you should pick on purpose, not by accident.
Erg Chebbi at a glance

items: Where: about 25 km from Erfoud, behind the village of Merzouga, near the Algerian border.
Size: a compact ridge roughly 22 km long, with crests rising about 150 metres.
Access: asphalt almost to the dunes — the easiest real Sahara in Morocco to reach.
Vibe: lively, well-serviced, endlessly photographed. Camps range from simple tents to luxury glamping with private bathrooms.
Good for: first-timers, families, short itineraries, and everyone on a Marrakech–Fès loop who wants the classic camel-at-sunset shot.

body.text: Erg Chigaga at a glance

items: Where: about 55 km of desert track past M'Hamid El Ghizlane, in the Draa valley region.
Size: a far bigger, lower-slung field of dunes — some crests climb well over double the height of Chebbi's.
Access: partly unpaved; the last stretch is 4x4 country. That remoteness is the whole point.
Vibe: silence, space, handfuls of camps. Fires, music, and no queue for the sunset viewpoint.
Good for: adventurous travelers, photographers, and anyone who bragged about getting off the beaten path.

body.text: Distance and access
From Marrakech, both dune fields are roughly a full day's drive (8–10 hours) — so the transfer day ends up being a highlight, not lost time.

To Erg Chebbi the road is tarmac the whole way, passing the Atlas mountains, Aït Ben Haddou, the Dades Gorges and the Todra Gorge — a scenic loop that fits perfectly into a [4-day Marrakech-to-Merzouga desert tour](/tours/atlas-to-sahara).

To Erg Chigaga you cross the Draa valley palm groves to Zagora, then drop south to M'Hamid, where the road ends. From there, a 4x4 carries you across stony desert to the dune field, passing nomad camps and the odd wild camel along the way.
The practical difference is simple: Chebbi is a day trip from Merzouga village; Chigaga is an expedition to the edge of the empty quarter.
Crowds and atmosphere

Erg Chebbi is Morocco's most-visited dune field — and for good reason: it is spectacular and easy. In October–April you will share the sunset ridge with other travelers. Merzouga has grown into a proper desert town with convenience stores, bike rentals, and dozens of camps.

Erg Chigaga is the opposite: even in high season, the dune field has very few camps and the silence is the headline. Sunrise typically means a wake-up call of hot tea and a companion who drives off after finding you a private dune. For couples and solo travelers chasing actual solitude, this is the clear winner.
Camel treks, activities and nights

items: Erg Chebbi: classic 1- to 2-hour camel treks to camp at sunset, sandboarding, quad bikes, Jeep tours — and an easy next-day sunrise before heading back to the road.

Erg Chigaga: longer, deeper treks — 2, 3, or more days of riding or walking across the dunes with a guide, camping each night in a wilder spot than the last. Sandboarding works even better on the taller, steeper slopes.

body.text: Both fields offer [stargazing camps](/tours/stargazing-night-camp), and both deserve a night or two — one night barely scratches the surface.
Price and tours

Erg Chebbi tours are cheaper on average, thanks to shared departures and competition. A [4-day Atlas-to-Sahara tour](/tours/atlas-to-sahara) or our [8-day grand Sahara loop](/tours/morocco-sahara-grand-tour-dunes-atlas) both spend a full day and nights at the dunes.

Erg Chigaga tours cost a little more because of the 4x4 transfers and remoteness — real value for your privacy. Try the [M'Hamid–Erg Chigaga 3-day trek](/tours/mhamid-erg-chigaga-3-day), or depart directly from [Marrakech](/tours/marrakech-erg-chigaga-4-day), [Ouarzazate](/tours/ouarzazate-erg-chigaga-3-day), or [Agadir](/tours/agadir-erg-chegaga-5-day) on 4- and 5-day desert tours that finish on the Chigaga dunes.
Which should you pick?

items: Pick Erg Chebbi if: first trip · 2–4 days only in the desert · traveling with kids · you want the most comfortable camps · you're combining the desert with the Atlas/Todra loop.
Pick Erg Chigaga if: you've done the touristy stuff in Morocco · you want real remoteness · long camel trekking appeals · queues and crowds kill the magic for you.
Mix them: add a [stargazing camp](/tours/stargazing-night-camp) at Chebbi or Chigaga for an extra unforgettable night — the sky over both is genuinely among the darkest you can sleep under.

body.text: Can you visit both in one trip?

Technically yes, but we would advise against it: the two dune fields sit about 450 km apart by road, and rushing from one to the other turns a dream trip into a transport exercise. Pick one and do it properly — you will carry the memory a lot longer than the itinerary.
Frequently asked questions

items.q: Which dunes are taller — Erg Chebbi or Erg Chigaga?
items.a: Erg Chigaga has the higher crests — individually less iconic, but collectively it climbs more. Erg Chebbi's dunes are famously photogenic but more compact.
The driving times are similar (8–10 hours), but Erg Chebbi is reachable entirely on asphalt, while Erg Chigaga needs an off-road 4x4 segment.

items.q: Are Erg Chebbi and Erg Chigaga both in the Sahara?
items.a: Yes. Both are true Saharan ergs (sand seas) in southeast Morocco, near the Algerian border — remote by European standards, routine for our team.

items.q: Which dune field is less touristy?
items.a: Erg Chigaga, without question. Its remoteness filters out the day-trippers, and its few camps rarely fill up.

items.q: What is the best time to visit the Moroccan desert?
items.a: October to April. The shoulder months (March and October) are the sweet spot — warm days, cool evenings, and clear skies for stargazing.

items.excerpt: A practical guide to choosing the right desert camp, arrival timing, and small comforts that make your first night unforgettable.
items.author: Sahara Vacation Team
items.title: How to plan a first Sahara night under the stars
items.content: The first trip into the desert is less about perfection and more about rhythm. Arrive in the late afternoon so the sky opens slowly, settle into a camp with a simple lantern-lit dinner, and leave a little time to walk quietly before the stars begin to dominate the sky. A good first desert night pairs warm mint tea, a local guide, and a clear plan for sunrise so nothing feels rushed.

items.excerpt: Luxury in the Sahara is rarely about marble. It is the soft details, warm hospitality, and the silence of a private camp at golden hour.
items.author: Amina Berrada
items.title: What makes a desert camp feel truly luxurious?
items.content: A luxury desert camp feels special when every touch point has intention. The tents are comfortable, the welcome is generous, and the experience is paced so guests can move from camel trek to tea ceremony to stargazing without ever feeling rushed. The best camps are built around stillness, with warm blankets, local food, and a view that says everything without a word.

items.excerpt: The desert is more than sand and sun. It is villages, music, families, and landscapes that unfold in layers over a single journey.
items.author: Walid El Azzouzi
items.title: Three ways to see the Sahara beyond the dunes
items.content: Travelers often arrive expecting a single horizon and leave with a deeper understanding of the oasis towns, caravan routes, and nomadic families who still shape desert life. You can explore this through a stargazing camp, a village music evening, or a four-day nomad immersion that unfolds at the pace of local stories.
